judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the third paragraph of the article body ("How a government elected on a promise..."), and it is entirely in English. I looked for a technique that would make it pass. The snapshot records a lang attribute only on html (pt-BR) and on the consent widget #didomi-host (en). The live HTML (Brazil edition) also has no lang anywhere except <html lang="pt-BR">. So the paragraph inherits pt-BR, and a screen reader would read English text with Portuguese rules. One objection is that English is the page's most-used language, so 3.1.1 (the html lang is wrong) is also implicated. That does not rescue the passage: its human language still cannot be programmatically determined correctly, which is what 3.1.2 requires.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the seventh paragraph of the article ("That is exactly what the Finch ruling allows..."), entirely in English. Neither the snapshot nor the live page has a lang attribute on the paragraph or on any ancestor other than <html lang="pt-BR">, so its programmatically determined language is pt-BR, which is wrong. No proper-name or vernacular exception applies to a whole paragraph. 3.1.1 is also arguably failed, since English is the most-used language on the page, but this passage's language is still misidentified, so the 3.1.2 claim holds.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the Creative Commons logo in the republish panel. I checked the crop, a screenshot crop and the SVG file itself: it shows the "cc creative commons" wordmark, without the BY and ND licence icons. The alt "CC BY ND" therefore says more than is drawn, but it names exactly what the logo is there to signal: the article is under a Creative Commons BY-ND licence, which the panel text confirms. 1.1.1 asks for a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, not a literal description of the pixels. Here the purpose (identifying the CC licence) is served and the extra detail is accurate. Requiring the alt to describe only what is visible is stricter than WCAG.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is an inline citation link in the sentence "Any challenge would most likely return to the Court of Session, where applications for judicial review normally must be made within three months." It points to legislation.gov.uk, section 89 of the Courts Reform (Scotland) Act 2014, which sets the judicial review time limit. The enclosing sentence, which is programmatically determined link context, makes clear that the link is the source for the three-month time limit, and the destination is consistent with that. The finding's statement that nothing around the link tells its purpose is wrong. This is a normal in-prose citation that passes 2.4.4 under technique G53.
